title: Days for everyone
hookLine: Eid is for the poor, the orphan, the traveler too

cards: Al-Bukhari keeps a sharp little saying, reported from Abu Hurayrah. In paraphrase: the worst food is the food of a wedding feast where the rich are invited and the poor are left out. Not spoiled food, not stolen food.
A good meal, at a happy party, with the wrong guest list. The saying is about a wedding. Some readers hear it about any feast, the two Eids included.
So, at the end of the festival year, a question about the guest list: who is Eid for?

teach.h: FOOD FOR THE POOR BEFORE THE PRAYER.
teach.b: Look at how the two Eids are built, and the guest list is written into them. Before Eid al-Fitr comes zakat al-fitr, the charity of the fast's end.

Ibn 'Abbas reports in Sunan Abi Dawud that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, made it a purification for the one who fasted and food for the poor, and that it counts as zakat when paid before the prayer.
Some read that timing as a way to make sure the poor eat on the feast day too. At Eid al-Adha, as yesterday, the meat leaves the house by design. Then the orphan.
Surah al-Insan praises people who, in Pickthall's words, "feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him."
A day of new clothes is a hard day for a child with no one to buy them, and some communities make a point of new clothes and gifts for orphans before Eid. Then the traveler.
The Qur'an names the wayfarer, the person far from home, among those owed kindness: on a feast day, the student who couldn't fly home, the new arrival, the night-shift worker.

And now the whole year we've walked: the sacred months, Muharram and Ashura, Rabi' al-Awwal, Rajab and Sha'ban, Ramadan from planning to the last ten, both Eids, Dhul Qa'dah's packing, Dhul Hijjah at home.

teach.h: A YEAR OF DAYS, ROOM AT THE TABLE.
teach.b: Each one, at its best, with room at the table.

how: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslims pay zakat al-fitr so that people in need can eat on the feast day, and at Eid al-Adha the meat of the sacrifice is shared with the poor; mosques and families often open their Eid meals to people who are alone, far from home or in need.

a festival year built with room for the poor

games.q: you're planning a big Eid meal. the guest list is full of family and friends who can host you back. what does the saying in al-Bukhari warn against?
o: a feast where the rich are invited and the poor are left out.
games.why: it calls that the worst food: a good meal, at a happy party, with the wrong guest list.

practice: Go slowly through the people you know, at work, on your street, in your family, and look for the one likely to spend the next holiday alone: a widowed neighbor, a colleague far from home, a student.
Let one face come, and picture the invitation, a meal, a coffee, a walk. If you pray, remember them by name; if not, hold the picture of the empty chair filled.

wordCard.voice: Days for everyone. The festival year built so that the poor eat, the orphan is dressed and the traveler is fed on the feast day too. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Qur'an's phrase for the wayfarer, the traveler far from home.

carryVoice: Your line: no one alone on eid. The table was always meant to have room. Next, a new stretch: many ways of being Muslim.
